title: Basic presentations: crossers and quartering targets
summary: What a trajectory is, how crossers and quartering targets fly, why they need different lead, and why you read a target from your own stand.

body.html: A trajectory is the path a target flies or rolls along. Coaches also say “presentation”: how the target is presented to the shooter. In Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ the trajectories copy the flight of game such as partridge, duck or pheasant. Compak® Sporting has varied trajectories too, but they are shorter.
Crossers fly across in front of you; quartering targets cross at an angle, going away from you or coming towards you.
body.heading: Watch how the target flies

body.html: This lesson covers crossers and quartering targets. Incomers and going-away targets are in Incomer, going-away, driven and overhead; teal, looper and other special ones are in Special presentations: teal, chandelle, looper and dropping targets.

A crosser flies more or less straight across your view, from one side to the other: left to right (written L→R) or right to left (R→L). On a Sporting™ layout the rules ask for a mix of crossing, quartering, incoming and going-away targets. In Compak® Sporting a left-to-right and a right-to-left crosser are two of the three compulsory trajectories, so each Compak field has them.

A crosser moves straight across your view, so all of its speed is sideways. That is why, at the same speed and distance, you need to shoot further in front of it than on other flight paths. This gap in front of the target is called lead (forward allowance): you fire at the place where the target is going to be, not where it is now. The faster the crosser and the further away it is, the more lead it needs. A “long crosser” means a far one, not one that flies for a long time.

Read its line and speed: does it fly flat, climb, or already drop at the break point (the spot where you plan to shoot it)? Does it show its face (the dome or the belly) or only its edge? Does it slow down? A slowing crosser needs less lead than one at full speed.

Many coaches teach a plan like this. Stand with your feet pointing to the spot where you will shoot, and find the target with your eyes early. Then keep the gun ahead of the target. You can start on the target and move ahead of it (pull-away). Or you can hold a steady gap in front of it from the start (maintained lead). Keep the gun moving as you fire. Both methods are explained in Lead: why you shoot in front of the target. After a missed crosser, coaches very often say “behind”: you were not far enough in front, or your gun stopped.
Directions are given from the shooter's point of view. If you stand facing the shooter, their “left to right” is your right to left, so do not turn the words round.

A quartering target flies at an angle: partly crossing, partly going away or coming in. Quartering away moves away from the shooter at an angle, for example out to the front right. Quartering towards (also “quartering in”) comes towards the shooter at an angle and passes to one side or drops in front. The angle can be anything between a straight target and a full crosser.

The lead depends on the angle. The closer the target is to flying straight away from you or straight at you, the less lead it needs. The closer it is to a full crosser, the more lead it needs, up to nearly as much as a crosser.

A quartering-away target gets smaller and slower quickly, so do not leave it too long. Many coaches suggest the pull-away method for it (start on the target, then move the gun ahead of it), because the gun stays on the target's line. Quartering towards grows bigger and looks slow, which tempts the shooter to wait; it can then pass too close or drop out of sight.

The same trap gives different presentations from different stands: from one stand a target is a crosser, from the next it is quartering. That is why targets must be read from the exact stand the shooter will use.

notes.html: Translate “quartering” by its meaning: an angled target going away from or coming towards the shooter. A word built literally from “quarter” means nothing to a shooter.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Long crosser, right to left — trust the lead and keep the gun moving.
phrases.meaning: The target is far away and flies from the shooter's right to left; give it the planned lead and do not stop the swing.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: You're behind it — give it more.
phrases.meaning: The shot passed behind the target: more lead is needed.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: It's dropping at your break point — stay under the line.
phrases.meaning: Where the shooter breaks it, the crosser is already falling, so the gun must travel slightly below its path.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Pick it up early, it's quick off the trap.
phrases.meaning: Look for the target closer to the trap than usual, because it leaves the trap fast.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: The first one's quartering away to the left — take it quickly before it gets small.
phrases.meaning: The first target moves away at an angle to the shooter's left; break it early.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Quartering in from the right — don't let it get too close.
phrases.meaning: The target comes towards the shooter at an angle from the right; do not wait for it.

phrases.speaker: coach
phrases.en: Less lead than you think — it's only a slight angle.
phrases.meaning: The target is nearly straight, so it needs only a small lead.

key_points.html: A trajectory is the target's path; a “presentation” is how it is shown to the shooter.
A crosser flies straight across your view: L→R or R→L.
At the same speed and distance a crosser needs the most lead (the gap you shoot in front of it); a quartering target needs less, depending on the angle.
Quartering away moves off at an angle; quartering towards (in) comes in at an angle.
One trap looks different from each stand: read it from your own stand.

did_you_know.html: Many Sporting™ presentation names come from hunting. Driven is the pheasant pushed towards the guns by beaters; teal is the small duck that springs almost straight up off the water.

quiz.q: Which presentation usually needs the most lead?

options.text: An incomer flying straight at the shooter
A crosser at the same distance

quiz.explain: All of a crosser's speed is sideways, so you shoot furthest in front of it; targets flying straight away from you or towards you need little sideways lead.

quiz.q: A target comes towards the shooter at an angle and passes to the side. What is it called?
quiz.explain: Quartering towards (or quartering in) is an angled target coming in; quartering away is the angled target moving off.

quiz.q: Why should a target be read from the exact stand you will shoot from?

options.text: One trap can give a different angle from each stand
The rules forbid watching from any other place
Targets change colour from one stand to the next
Only the referee may stand anywhere else

quiz.explain: The angle between the shooter and the target's line changes with the position, so the presentation changes too.
